statutes_cited: Section 2(8) of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891
holding: For the foregoing reasons, the applications for leave to defend filed by defendants No.1, 3, 4 and 5 and defendant No.2 are dismissed, and the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff-bank and against the defendants jointly and severally for a sum of Rs.132,335,304.66 (Rupees One Hundred Thirty-Two Million Three Hundred Thirty-Five Thousand Three Hundred Four and Sixty-Six Paisas Only), along with costs of the suit and cost of funds as envisaged in Section 3 of the Ordinance, 2001, on the defaulted amount from 31.12.2024 till the date of actual realization of the decretal amount. The decretal amount shall be recoverable, inter alia, through the sale of the mortgaged, pledged and hypothecated properties of the defendants, strictly in accordance with law. No relief is granted against the proforma defendants No.6 & 7. Decree sheet be drawn accordingly.

paragraphs.text: Date of hearing: 05.11.2026. Plaintiff by: Mr. Muhammad Nadeem, Advocate. Defendants by: M/s. Amir Wakeel Butt and Asifa Amir Butt, Advocates (for defendants No.1,3 & 4) Ch. Sohail Khurshid, Advocate (for defendant No.2). Barrister Muhammad Imran Ramzan, Advocate (for defendant No.6-UBL). MUHAMMAD SAJID MEHMOOD SETHI, J.- Through the instant suit instituted under Section 9 of the Financial Institutions (Recovery of Finances) Ordinance, 2001 (“the Ordinance, 2001”), the plaintiff-bank seeks recovery of an amount aggregating to Rs.132,335,304.66 (Rupees One Hundred Thirty-Two Million Three Hundred Thirty-Five Thousand Three Hundred Four and Sixty-Six Paisas Only), comprising principal of Rs.92,000,000/- and deferred Istisna income of Rs.40,335,304.66, along with cost of funds from 30.09.2024 till realization, through sale of the mortgaged and charged properties, against the defendant-company, its directors and guarantors, on account of Istisna Finance Facility, which is a sub-limit of Rs.190,000,000/- under the Murabaha/Import facility.

The case of the plaintiff-bank, as borne out from the record, is that defendants No.1 to 5 availed a fresh Murabaha/Import Facility of Rs.190,000,000/- under the Murabaha Facility Agreement dated 26.10.2018 and its sub-limit Istisna Finance of Rs.190,000,000/- on the strength of Board Resolution dated 26.10.2018 and request letter dated 11.05.2018. The facility was sanctioned through offer letter dated 26.10.2018 and regulated through a comprehensive set of banking instruments executed by the defendants, including Demand Promissory Note, Murabaha Facility Agreement, Istisna Agreement and undertakings (all dated 26.10.2018). The facility was secured through personal guarantees of defendants No.2 to 4 dated 26.10.2018; a mortgage deed executed on 20.07.2019, registered with the Sub- Registrar, Ferozewala on 22.07.2019, vide document No.11491, Jild No.6223, in respect of 5-Kanal land bearing Khewat No.442, Khatoni No.1007, situated at Hadbast Mouza Thatha Khuda Yar, Tehsil Ferozewala, District Sheikhupura; a mortgage charge certificate of Rs.383.387 million registered with the SECP; a Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds dated 12.06.2019 together with Mutation No.14873 sanctioned on 30.09.2019; the original title documents; and a hypothecation charge of Rs.254 million with the SECP, with no- objection certificates of other banks.

The plaintiff-bank further pleads that the Istisna facility was renewed five times: through offer letters dated 07.01.2020, 09.11.2020, 22.10.2021, 30.01.2023 and, finally, offer letter dated 23.10.2023, each accepted by the Chief Executive of the defendant- company by sign and stamp and each accompanied by fresh instruments, including, in the last renewal, the Demand Promissory Note, Master Istisna Agreement, Istisna (Master) Agency Agreement and Istisna Corporate Guarantee, all dated 23.10.2023, and the personal guarantees of defendants No.2 to 5 of the same date. The last renewal was preceded by Form-A, Board Resolution dated 11.08.2023 and request letter dated 18.08.2023. By para 24 of the plaint, the plaintiff-bank has confined the suit to Facility No.2/Istisna, the remaining facilities having been adjusted. It is pleaded that the defendants failed to repay on expiry of the facility on 30.09.2024, that a demand notice dated 20.12.2024 was served upon them, and that, as a result of default, Rs.132,335,304.66 stands outstanding as per the statement of account of Istisna Financing and the statement of Deferred Istisna Income, both certified under the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891.

Defendants No.1, 3, 4 and 5 sought leave to defend under Section 10 of the Ordinance, 2001. Their defence, as pleaded, is that no Istisna price was ever paid to them against any goods; that they never requested the renewal of 23.10.2023 nor executed its documents; and that the entire suit amount is disputed. The statement required by Section 10(4) of the Ordinance, 2001 is "Nil/Nil", and no document or statement of account was annexed with the application. Defendant No.2 filed a separate application for leave to defend the suit by raising similar plea, however he also did not provide any details as contemplated under Section 10(4) of the Ordinance, 2001 and repeated “Nil/Nil”, without any supporting document. During the proceedings, a local commission was also appointed, which submitted its report, and the plaintiff-bank filed objections thereto.

Learned counsel for the plaintiff-bank submits that the defendants have failed to comply with Sections 10(4) and 10(5) of the Ordinance, 2001, having neither traversed the statements of account specifically nor disclosed any precise amount in dispute nor annexed any document or statement of their own account, and are, therefore, disentitled to leave to defend in terms of Sections 10(1) and 10(6) of the Ordinance, 2001. He submits that the Istisna facility was sanctioned and repeatedly renewed with the acknowledgment of the defendants themselves through their request letters dated 11.05.2018, 24.08.2021 and 18.08.2023, and that the defendants rely only upon the fourth and fifth renewals without saying a word about the original facility and the first three renewals. He contends that the plaint complies with Section 9(3) through para 28 and the certified statements of account, which bear the stamp and signature of the concerned bank officer and are certified in terms of Section 2(8) of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, and therefore comply with Section 9(2); that the defendants have not impugned a single entry in the statements of account and are barred by the doctrine of financial estoppel from doing so; that the plea of non-disbursement is baseless as disbursements were made strictly on the written requests of the defendants; and that the guarantors' liability is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor. He prays that the applications seeking leave to defend the suit be dismissed and the suit decreed as prayed for. In support, she has relied upon Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. and others v. Soneri Bank Ltd. (PLD 2012 Supreme Court 268), Muhammad Saleem Khan v. MCB Bank Limited (2020 SCMR 984), Baba Fareed Ghee Industries (Pvt.) Limited through Chief Executive and 3 others v. National Bank of Pakistan (2002 CLD 669), International Finance Corporation v. Sarah Textile Ltd. and 3 others (2009 CLD 761), Qalab Hussain v. Faysal Bank and others (2017 CLD 215), Messrs Naeem Zafar Industries and others v. Bank of Punjab (2017 CLD 397), National Bank of Pakistan v. Messrs Naseem Enterprises and Trading (Pvt.) Limited and others (2026 CLD 1104) and National Bank of Pakistan v. Chenab Limited and others (2017 CLD 1539).

Conversely, learned counsel for the defendants submits, in the written submissions filed on behalf of defendants No.1, 3, 4 and 5, that the suit is liable to be rejected or, at the very least, the defendants are entitled to unconditional leave to defend with the question of maintainability framed as a preliminary issue, on the following grounds: (i) the plaintiff-bank has confined the suit to the Istisna facility, which is a sale and not a loan; the Master Istisna Agreement dated 23.10.2023 creates obligations only under an identified Istisna Transaction constituted by a Written Offer and Acceptance of Offer; the plaint identifies no such transaction, goods, Contract Price, delivery date, failure to deliver, notice or sale, and instead pleads a failure to repay principal and markup, which is not an obligation under an Istisna; the plaint also pleads inconsistent dates of default (18.09.2024 in para 28 and 30.09.2024 in para 30); hence there is no default and no cause of action under Section 9(1) of the Ordinance, 2001 and the plaint is liable to rejection under Order VII Rule 11(a), C.P.C.; (ii) on the plaintiff-bank's own statement (Annex V, pages 466 to 469), the balance sued for consists of entries of "Istisna Financing Against Agreement" dated between 22.05.2024 and 28.06.2024, which on a tenor of 180 days could not have matured before mid- November to late December 2024, whereas the Master Agreement was valid until 31.12.2024; (iii) Section 9(2) is not complied with because, besides the statement of account, the "relevant documents relating to the grant of finance", namely Written Offers, Acceptances, transaction-wise promissory notes, proof of payment of Contract Price, Goods Receiving Notes and sale documents, have not been filed, and the statement is not certified as the certificate at page 469 is a printed paragraph without name, designation, date or signature; (iv) Section 9(3) is not complied with because para 28 states a limit instead of the finance availed, refers to the statement of account instead of stating the repayments and their dates, and states a split between principal and deferred income that cannot be derived from the statement; (v) the Istisna being a sale, no profit or "Deferred Istisna Income" can accrue before sale of goods, late-payment amounts are payable to the Charity Fund and not to the bank, and mark-up on mark-up is prohibited, in view of the Essentials of Istisna issued by the State Bank of Pakistan (IBD Circular No.02 of 2008), AAOIFI Shariah Standards No.11 and No.25 adopted through IBD Circular No.01 of 2022, IBD Circular No.01 of 2018 and BCD Circulars No.13 and No.32 of 1984; and (vi) the Master Istisna Agreement is for Rs.250 million against a limit of Rs.190 million. Learned counsel has relied upon Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. and others v. Soneri Bank Ltd. (PLD 2012 Supreme Court 268), Bankers Equity Limited through Principal Law Officer and 5 others v. Messrs Bentonite Pakistan Limited and 7 others (2003 CLD 931), The Bank of Punjab v. Fazal Abbas and another (2020 CLD 977) and Jamal Tube (Pvt.) Ltd., Lahore through Chief Executive Officer and others v. First Punjab Modaraba, Lahore through Authorized Officer and another (2021 CLD 1372).
Arguments heard. Record perused. Questions for determination

The following questions arise for determination: (a) whether the suit has been competently instituted by an authorised officer of the plaintiff-bank; (b) whether the applications for leave to defend comply with Sections 10(3) to 10(6) of the Ordinance, 2001; (c) whether the plaint is supported by a duly certified statement of account and by the relevant documents relating to the grant of finance as required by Section 9(2) of the Ordinance, 2001 and Section 2(8) of the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891; (d) whether Section 9(3) is complied with; (e) whether the plaint discloses a cause of action under Section 9(1) and is liable to rejection under Order VII Rule 11, C.P.C.; (f) whether the defences of non-disbursement, non-execution, the sanctioned limit and illegality of profit raise any substantial question of law or fact requiring evidence; and (g) the quantum of the decree, including the date of default and the base on which cost of funds is to be awarded, and the liability of each defendant. Scheme of Sections 9 and 10 of the Ordinance, 2001

Both sides rely principally on Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. supra, and rightly so, for it lays the foundation of the procedure under the Ordinance, 2001. The Supreme Court held that Sections 9 and 10 require strict compliance and are mandatory, and that the Ordinance, 2001 binds both sides to be absolutely specific on accounts so that controversies are confined to the claimed and the disputed numbers. The mandatory character of these provisions is, however, a two-way street: it requires a financial institution to support its plaint in the manner prescribed by Section 9, and equally requires a defendant who seeks leave to defend to satisfy Section 10. The Court is also duty- bound, as held in the same judgment, to examine for itself whether the suit complies with Section 9, even where the defendant has failed to obtain leave. This Court will, therefore, first examine the defendants' own compliance with Section 10 and then, without relying upon that failure alone, examine every objection raised against the plaint, so that the decision rests on both footings. Authority to institute the suit

The defendants have also questioned the competency of the suit and the authority of the person who instituted it. Such an objection, if well founded, would go to the root of maintainability and is, therefore, dealt with at the outset. The Ordinance, 2001 is a special law, and the legislative intent is to avoid hyper-technical objections and to ensure expeditious adjudication and recovery of public money. The superior Courts have consistently held that a duly executed or registered power of attorney is, by itself, sufficient proof of lawful authority and requires no further corroboration, such as a board resolution, and that even a branch manager alone is competent to institute such proceedings. Reliance in this regard may be placed on First Dawood Investment Bank Ltd. v. Bank Islami Pakistan Ltd. (2019 SCMR 1925), The Bank of Punjab v. Messrs Magic River Services and 4 others (2016 CLD 171), Messrs RAVI Medical Supplies (Pvt.) Limited through Chief Executive and 4 others v. Messrs First Women Bank Limited through Branch Manager (2016 CLD 1726), Bank of Punjab v. Poly Pack Pvt. Limited and others (2017 CLD 1285), Messrs Bahawalpur Cotton Company v. United Bank Limited (2021 CLD 434) and The Bank of Khyber through Branch Manager v. Messrs Kashmir Sugar Mills Limited through Chief Executive and others (2021 CLD 1220). In the present case, the suit has been instituted by an officer of the plaintiff-bank on the strength of a valid and subsisting power of attorney placed on record, which fulfils all legal requirements and has not been shown to suffer from any infirmity. The objection is, therefore, misconceived and is repelled. Non-compliance with Sections 10(4) and 10(5) of the Ordinance, 2001

The law obligates a defendant to specifically traverse the statements of account filed by the financial institution and to disclose precise amounts disputed, supported by relevant documents and a statement of his own account. A careful examination of the defendants' applications for leave to defend reveals non-compliance with the mandatory requirements of Sections 10(4) and 10(5) of the Ordinance, 2001. In the present case, the only statement offered under Section 10(4) is "Nil/Nil". Such an entry is not a statement of finance availed, repaid and outstanding; it is a bare denial of the whole claim. The defendants have not stated what, if anything, they received under the Istisna facility in the years 2018 to 2024, what they paid, what they say is the correct outstanding balance, or which entry out of the 73 pages of the principal statement and the 104 pages of the deferred income statement is incorrect and why. Nor have they annexed with their applications a single document, whether a bank statement of defendant No.1, an audited account, a payment record or even a counter-statement. The plea that no Istisna price was paid is a matter peculiarly within the knowledge of the defendants, who would have the record of their own bank accounts and books; it cannot be raised and then left unsupported by any material. A general denial, which neither admits nor specifies any amount, raises no substantial question of law or fact requiring evidence, and the special procedure under the Ordinance, 2001 does not permit a defendant to obtain leave in the hope of finding a defence at trial. Bald assertions in an application for leave to defend, without the backing of audited accounts or any document of the defendant-company, cannot be given credence. Their defence remains general, evasive and unsupported by any independent material. Such failure attracts the consequences contemplated under Sections 10(1) and 10(6) of the Ordinance, 2001, disentitling them from the grant of leave to defend. Reliance in this regard may be placed on Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. and others v. Soneri Bank Ltd. (PLD 2012 Supreme Court 268), Habib Metropolitan Bank Limited through Attorney v. Century 21 Textile and Sportswear (Pvt.) Limited and 3 others (2014 CLD 729), Silk Bank Limited through Authorized Persons v. Messrs AZM Chemical Company through Proprietor and 5 others (2014 CLD 1526) and Al-Madina Aluminium Work and others v. Habib Metropolitan Bank (2020 CLD 892). Statements of account: certification under Section 9(2) of the Ordinance, 2001 and Section 2(8) of the Bankers’ Books Evidence Act, 1891.

Nevertheless, as the defendants have challenged the very maintainability of the suit, and as this Court is itself obliged to examine compliance with Section 9, the remaining objections are dealt with on merit. The first is that the statement of account is not certified under Section 2(8) of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891 because the certificate at page 469 is a printed paragraph bearing no name, designation, date or signature, and because the statement itself recites that it is computer generated and does not carry a signature.

This Court has perused pages 397 to 469 (Statement of Account of Istisna Financing) and pages 470 to 573 (Statement of Deferred Istisna Income). Every page of both statements bears the stamp of the bank and the signature of the bank officer Mr. Ishfaq Ahmad Mugha, as well as the signature and stamp of Mr. Sajjad Sarwar, Vice President of the plaintiff-bank. The certificates at pages 469 and 573 state that the entries are true copies of entries in the ordinary books of the bank, made in the usual and ordinary course of business, and that the books are in the custody of the bank; they are dated and subscribed by the officer with his name and designation. The statement that a computer printout "does not carry any signature" is a generic footer printed on system-generated statements; it does not detract from a separate certificate appended at the foot of the statement, signed by the competent officer. The statements are, therefore, duly certified in strict compliance with Section 2(8) of the Bankers' Books Evidence Act, 1891, which requires certification by a competent bank officer confirming that the entries are true copies made in the ordinary course of banking business. Once a statement is so certified, objections as to its format, mode of printout or internal references do not render it inadmissible or unreliable, and the plea that the statements are fake or unreliable is equally misconceived. The law is well settled that duly certified bank statements carry a statutory presumption of correctness and constitute prima facie evidence of liability. In the absence of any effective rebuttal, such statements are sufficient to establish the outstanding dues. The defendants have failed to produce any credible material to displace this presumption. No material has been produced to show that any entry is fabricated or does not pertain to the subject facility. Reference is made to Muhammad Saleem Khan v. MCB Bank Limited (2020 SCMR 984), Messrs Habib Metropolitan Bank Limited v. Messrs Faizan Ali and Company (Pvt.) Ltd. through Chief Executive Officer and others (2017 CLD 1583), First Dawood Investment Bank Limited v. New Allied Electronics (PVT.) Limited and another (2018 CLD 250), Trust Investment Bank Limited v. The Bank of Punjab (2021 CLD 1430) and MCB Bank Limited through Authorized Officer v. Messrs City Steel UAE Mills (Pvt.) Ltd. through Chief Executive and others (2024 CLD 387). Statements of account: "all other relevant documents relating to the grant of finance"

The principal thrust of the defence is that, for an Istisna, "the finance is granted" only upon an accepted Written Offer for specific goods and payment of the Contract Price, so that Written Offers, Acceptances, Goods Receiving Notes, transaction-wise promissory notes and sale documents were the "relevant documents" which the plaintiff-bank was obliged to file with the plaint. The submission is ingenious, but it is not sustainable.

Section 9(2) requires the plaint to be supported by a certified statement of account and by “all other relevant documents relating to the grant of finance”. The purpose is to enable the customer to know the amount advanced, the basis of the claim and the nature of default, so that his defence is not rendered illusory. The expression “relevant documents” must, therefore, be read in the light of this purpose; it encompasses documents constituting and evidencing the grant of finance and the customer's liability, rather than every operational paper generated in the course of a drawdown. Such documents include the sanction and offer letters, the customer's request letters and board resolutions, the finance and master agreements, promissory notes, guarantees and security documents. In the present case, the original financing arrangement was sanctioned and regulated through the Murabaha Facility Agreement dated 26.10.2018, while the specific Istisna component forming the subject matter of the present suit was governed by the Istisna Agreement of the same date, together with the relevant promissory notes, undertakings and security documents. The plaintiff-bank has filed these documents for the original grant of 2018 as well as for each of the five subsequent renewals, as detailed in paragraphs 2 and 3 above, together with the principal statement of account reflecting each drawdown under the description “Istisna Financing Against Agreement”, along with its date and agreement number. The decree in Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. supra was sustained because the documents relating to the grant of finance, securities and statements of account in respect of each facility had been duly filed; the plaintiff-bank has, on the record before this Court, substantially demonstrated the same compliance.

The Master Istisna Agreement dated 23.10.2023 is itself a document executed by the defendants and records that the manufacturer has offered to manufacture goods from time to time and that Istisna Transactions would be entered into during its tenor from 23.10.2023 to 31.12.2024. The Written Offers and Acceptances are documents executed between the parties for the mechanics of each drawdown; they are, in the very nature of things, signed by the officers of the defendant-company itself and are within its knowledge and record. The defendants do not say, with reference to any entry, that a particular drawdown was not made, that a particular Written Offer was not signed by them, or that any particular Contract Price did not reach their account. In the absence of any such specific plea, the omission to annex each transaction-level paper does not make the plaint incomplete in the sense of Section 9(2). The defendants' submission, if accepted, would require a bank to annex hundreds of operational papers for every drawdown in every case of Islamic finance, which is not what the Legislature has demanded and would defeat the object of the Ordinance, 2001 as a special law for the expeditious recovery of finance.

The Court has also kept in view that the offer letters, master agreements and agency agreements are not mere umbrella papers. Each of the defendants' own request letters dated 11.05.2018, 24.08.2021 and 18.08.2023 acknowledges the Istisna finance facility of Rs.190,000,000/-; the facility was accepted each year by the Chief Executive of the defendant-company with sign and stamp; and the last renewal was preceded by the company's board resolution dated 11.08.2023. The defendants have not denied the original facility or the first three renewals at all, as the plaintiff-bank rightly points out; their written submissions rely only upon the fourth and fifth renewals. Their own written submissions record that the entries making up the claim bear dates from 22.05.2024 to 28.06.2024. These drawdowns were made after the expiry of the fourth renewal on 30.09.2023 and can only have been made under the fifth renewal. The defendants cannot say that they never asked for or accepted the renewal of 23.10.2023 and at the same time maintain that these entries, which could have been made only under it, are unexplained.

Reliance on Jamal Tube (Pvt.) Ltd. supra is misplaced. The judgment turned on its own facts, where it was admitted that the bank had not appended with the plaint complete documents or statements of account showing disbursement of the amounts in the account of the customer, and the customer's case was that the entries were cosmetic transactions made only to show disbursement. The ratio is that a bank which omits the relevant documents relating to the grant of finance cannot cure the omission later; it is not that a bank must annex in every Islamic-finance case each transaction paper before the plaint can be entertained. Here the plaint is supported by the complete chain of financing and security documents of every year, by the defendants' own request letters and board resolutions, and by statements showing each drawdown by date and agreement number. The plea of "cosmetic entries" is nowhere supported even by a single bank statement of the defendant-company showing that the credits never reached it. The authority is, therefore, distinguishable.

The plea regarding alleged non-disbursement of the Istisna finance is without any substance. The record clearly reflects that disbursements were made in accordance with the written requests of the defendants and are supported by the certified entries in the banking books. It is well settled that entries made in banking books maintained in the ordinary course of business carry inherent reliability, and a mere denial cannot override the statutory presumption attached thereto. Reference may be made to National Bank of Pakistan v. Messrs Naseem Enterprises and Trading (Pvt.) Limited and others (2026 CLD 1104). Non-challenge of entries in the statements of account; financial estoppel

The defendants have failed to impugn any entry of the statements of account in their applications. It is not enough to say that the whole amount is disputed. The Ordinance, 2001 requires the defendant to raise a specific objection against specific entries. In the case of Sarah Textile Ltd. supra, the Court held as under:- "9…. Appraisal of record appended with the plaint clearly reflects that the statement of accounts appended with the plaint is in accordance with the parameters of Section 9 of the Ordinance 2001, there absolutely is no ambiguity in the same. It has been certified, as required under the law, the defendants have not objected to any specific entry in this context, they were required under the law to raise a specific objection, but it was not done, as evident from the contents of PLA, as such they cannot now raise this issue under the principle of 'secundum allegata et probata'. It is imperative to state here that the defendants denied liability in law and not on facts, as they did not deny the execution of documents subject to present dispute…."

The attempt of the defendants to dispute the correctness of the statements of account is also devoid of legal force. The doctrine of financial estoppel, as crystallized in the cases of Chenab Limited and Messrs Naeem Zafar Industries supra squarely applies to the present case. It has been consistently held that where banking customers receive periodic statements of account and fail to raise timely objections, they are estopped from subsequently disputing their correctness. In the present case, the defendants neither raised any contemporaneous objection nor produced any counter statement to dislodge the entries reflected in the plaintiff-bank's record. Consequently, they are legally precluded from challenging the veracity of the accounts at this belated stage.

The attempt of the defendants to isolate selective entries while ignoring the complete transactional chain (as in their reliance on the entries dated 22.05.2024 to 28.06.2024 alone) is also legally untenable. It is well settled that banking transactions cannot be dissected in isolation but must be examined in their entirety as reflected in the continuous account maintained in the ordinary course of business. The statements placed on record are integrated accounts reflecting all debit and credit entries, including drawdowns, repayments and profit, in chronological sequence. The law does not require a fragmented or separately tabulated disclosure once the entire transactional history is available through a duly certified statement maintained in the ordinary course of banking business. Reference may be made to CITIBANK N.A. through Duly Authorized Attorney v. Sana Ullah (Pvt.) Limited and 4 others (2016 CLD 1448) and First Dawood Investment Bank Limited v. New Allied Electronics (Pvt.) Limited and another (2018 CLD 250). Section 9(3) of the Ordinance, 2001

The objection of non-compliance with Section 9(3) is equally misconceived. Para 28 of the plaint states the Istisna Finance Limit of Rs.190,000,000/-, states that the entries in statement of account No.19537-714-0173751 are an essential part of the plaint, and states the amount payable as Rs.92,000,000/- principal together with Rs.40,335,304.66 deferred Istisna income, in all Rs.132,335,304.66. The certified statement at page 469 shows the outstanding balance of the Istisna financing as Rs.132,335,304.66 on 18.09.2024 after repayments, which comprises the principal of Rs.92,000,000/- and the deferred Istisna income of Rs.40,335,304.66 shown separately in the certified statement at page 573. The position is, therefore, as under:- Sr. No. Nature Principal Deferred Istisna Income Total Outstanding 1. Istisna Finance Facility Rs.92,000,000/- Rs.40,335,304.66 Rs.132,335,304.66

The purpose of Section 9(3), as explained in Apollo Textile Mills Ltd. supra, is that the controversy be confined to the claimed and disputed numbers. That purpose is fully served when the plaint states the claim by amount, and incorporates, as an essential part of the plaint, a certified statement showing each disbursement and each payment by date. The defendants have not been prejudiced in any manner; they have been able to formulate the very objection they now take. To insist that the repayments and dates be retyped in the body of the plaint when they appear in the statement relied upon in the same paragraph would be to prefer form over substance. As to the objection that the amount payable must be stated up to the date of institution of the suit, the plaintiff-bank has claimed the balance as on 18.09.2024 and has separately claimed cost of funds thereafter, which accrues by operation of Section 3 of the Ordinance, 2001 till realization; nothing is, therefore, left unstated. The extent to which cost of funds is actually awarded is dealt with in the paragraphs on quantum below. Cause of action under Section 9(1) and Order VII Rule 11, C.P.C.

It is next contended that the plaint discloses no default in fulfilment of any obligation and, therefore, no cause of action, because under the Master Istisna Agreement the customer's only obligation is to manufacture and deliver and, on default, to refund the Contract Price after notice under clause 10.02. The plaint has to be read as a whole together with its annexures, as held in Haji Abdul Karim and others v. Messrs Florida Builders (Pvt.) Limited (PLD 2012 Supreme Court 247). That principle cuts against the defendants. So read, the plaint discloses the following: a finance in the form of Istisna Facility No.2 of Rs.190,000,000/-, sanctioned and renewed for six years, the last renewal expiring on 30.09.2024; advances made thereunder and recorded in the certified statement; an obligation of the customer to pay back what was advanced together with the agreed profit at the end of the transaction tenor and on expiry of the facility; a failure to do so; a demand notice dated 20.12.2024; and the institution of this suit thereafter. An "obligation" under Section 2(e) of the Ordinance, 2001 includes any agreement for the repayment or extension of time in repayment of a finance, or for its renewal, and all covenants made by the customer. The offer letter of 23.10.2023, the request letters of the defendants seeking the renewal, the Demand Promissory Note, the Master Istisna Agreement, the Agency Agreement, and the guarantees constitute exactly such an obligation. Under the Agency Agreement the defendant-company, as the agent of the bank, was bound to sell the goods and cause the buyers to remit the sale price directly to the bank; the plaint says that it did not. The Court cannot hold that a customer who has taken Rs.92,000,000/- from the bank under a renewed Istisna facility, and has not paid it on expiry of the facility and after a demand notice, has committed no default.

The inconsistency between the dates of default in paras 28 and 30 is also of no consequence. The date of 18.09.2024 is the date up to which the statement was struck, and 30.09.2024 is the date of expiry of the facility from which cost of funds is claimed. Pleading of dates in a plaint is a matter of particulars, not of the essence of the cause of action, and does not displace a cause of action that otherwise stands disclosed. The defendants' own computation shows that every drawdown dated between 22.05.2024 and 28.06.2024 had matured, even on a 180-day tenor, by 25.12.2024, and the Master Istisna Agreement had run its tenor by 31.12.2024. The suit was instituted in March 2025, when every transaction had matured, the facility had expired, the demand notice had been served and the defendants had still not paid. Default had thus been committed in respect of every transaction before institution of the suit, and that is all that Section 9(1) requires. The defendants' timeline point is, therefore, relevant only to the date from which cost of funds is to be awarded, which has been dealt with in the paragraphs on quantum below, and not to the maintainability of the suit.

Order VII Rule 11, C.P.C. is a drastic remedy, and the plaint can be rejected under it only where, on a bare reading of the plaint and its annexures, no cause of action is disclosed. That is not the case here. Moreover, the objection is raised in the guise of a plea that the transaction-level documents are missing, which is a matter of evidence and is, as shown above, answered by the record. The defendants have not shown any ground for rejection of the plaint. The prayer for framing a preliminary issue of maintainability is likewise declined, as no such issue is called for where the objections are themselves decided on the face of the record. Sanctioned limit and the Master Istisna Agreement

The last objection of the defendants, that the Master Istisna Agreement is for Rs.250 million whereas the sanctioned limit is Rs.190 million, does not advance their case either. The plaintiff-bank has sued only on the Istisna Finance Facility (Facility No.2), and the principal claimed, Rs.92,000,000/-, is well within the sanctioned limit of Rs.190,000,000/-. A higher ceiling recorded in the agreement may, at the most, bear upon what the bank could have advanced beyond the sanctioned limit; it furnishes no ground for resisting repayment of the amount shown to have been advanced, which lies within the limit sanctioned by the offer letters and accepted by the defendants. The objection raises no question requiring evidence and is repelled. Nature of Istisna; SBP instructions; Shariah objections

The defendants have devoted a large part of their submissions to the juristic nature of Istisna, to the Essentials of Istisna prescribed by the State Bank of Pakistan through IBD Circular No.02 of 2008, to AAOIFI Shariah Standards No.11 and No.25 adopted through IBD Circular No.01 of 2022, to IBD Circular No.01 of 2018 and to BCD Circulars No.13 and No.32 of 1984, to contend that no profit accrues on an Istisna until the manufactured goods are sold and that late-payment amounts must go to charity. This Court has considered these submissions with care. They do not, however, provide a defence to the claim.

Firstly, the Ordinance, 2001 itself, in Section 2(d), includes in "finance" an accommodation or facility provided on the basis of purchase and sale of any property including commodities, musharika, morabaha, musawama, istisnah or modaraba certificate, in addition to loans, advances and other financial accommodations. A suit under Section 9 for recovery of an Istisna finance is, therefore, a suit on a finance within the meaning of the Ordinance. The question whether the bank's product structure conforms to the essentials of Istisna is one between the bank and its regulator, the State Bank of Pakistan, which has prescribed penal consequences for non-compliance, and the Shariah Board of the bank; it is not a defence for a customer who has taken the money and used it. The circulars regulate the conduct of the Islamic banking institutions; none of them provides that a customer is absolved from returning the funds that he has actually received from the bank. This Court, exercising the special jurisdiction under the Ordinance, 2001, is also not the forum to declare a facility, availed by the defendants and renewed by them year after year for six years, void on Shariah grounds, which question the Constitution has placed before the Federal Shariat Court and the Shariat Appellate Bench of the Supreme Court. Having enjoyed the benefit of the facility, and having applied for its renewal on the very terms of the Master Istisna Agreement, the defendants are estopped by the principle of approbation and reprobation from now taking a position contrary to the contract they signed. Reliance is placed upon Messrs Naeem Zafar Industries and others v. Bank of Punjab (2017 CLD 397).

Secondly, the apprehension that profit may have been charged before sale of the goods, or that late-payment amounts belong to the Charity Fund, is a matter that goes to the quantum of the profit component and not to the existence of the liability for the principal. The decree, as explained below, awards no profit beyond the deferred Istisna price which the defendants contractually agreed to pay. The contention that cost of funds amounts to mark-up on mark-up within the meaning of BCD Circulars No.13 and No.32 of 1984 is addressed in para 37. Execution of documents, denial of renewal and plea of forgery

The defendants deny having requested the renewal of 23.10.2023 and having executed its documents. This denial is wholly unsupported. The renewal was preceded by a board resolution of the defendant-company dated 11.08.2023, Form-A and a request letter dated 18.08.2023 (page 310), all emanating from the defendant- company for renewal of existing credit facility line with some modification; the offer letter bears the sign and stamp of its Chief Executive; and, as noticed in para 18 above, the drawdowns on which the suit is based were made in May and June 2024 and could only have been made under that renewal. The defendants have not alleged who forged what, how, or when, have not particularized any forgery, have not sought any handwriting or forensic examination, have not initiated any proceedings against any official of the bank, and have not disputed the earlier years' documents. A bare plea of forgery, unsupported by any legal proceedings or evidence, is insufficient to dislodge contractual liability. The burden to prove forgery lies heavily upon the party alleging it, which the defendants have failed to discharge. Liability of the defendants

With regard to the liability of defendant No.1 as principal borrower, the documentary record is overwhelming and unambiguous. The offer letters, the Master Istisna Agreements, the Board Resolutions, the Mortgage Deed, the charge registered with the SECP and the Memorandum of Deposit of Title Deeds collectively establish the execution, availment, acknowledgment and continuation of liability. The conduct of the defendant-company, including its repeated requests for renewal and extension of time, further reinforces the subsistence of the liability. Defendant No.1 is, therefore, fully and squarely liable. Defendants No.2 to 5 are continuing guarantors under the personal guarantees dated 23.10.2023 and the earlier guarantees of each renewal. The settled principle of law, reiterated in Qalab Hussain supra, is that the liability of a guarantor is co-extensive with that of the principal debtor and remains enforceable so long as the principal liability subsists. The Istisna Corporate Guarantee dated 23.10.2023 was likewise executed pursuant to a board resolution and the contractual arrangements between the parties, and no material has been produced to rebut it. The defendant-company has also created a registered mortgage, a memorandum of deposit of title deeds, and charges with the SECP, which are continuing securities to secure all present and future liabilities until full satisfaction of the dues, and they are enforceable in law. The defendant-company, as mortgagor and chargor, remains liable to the extent of the mortgaged and charged security. Overall appreciation

From an overall appreciation of the record, this Court is of the considered view that the plaintiff-bank has established its claim through voluminous and duly certified documentary record forming a coherent and consistent chain from the original sanction in 2018 to the last renewal of 2023 and carrying a statutory presumption of correctness, and that the liability of the defendants is supported by their own request letters and board resolutions. In contrast, the defence raised is vague, unsupported, and contradictory, and thus falls short of the standard required in proceedings under the Ordinance, 2001, which are summary in nature and intended for expeditious recovery of financial liabilities.

From the overall tenor of the defence, it is evident that no substantial question of law or fact has been raised which would necessitate the recording of evidence. The objections taken are either purely technical, already addressed hereinabove, or unsupported by any cogent material. It is well settled that leave to defend cannot be granted as a matter of course and must be founded upon a bona fide and substantial defence, which is conspicuously absent in the present case. The case law relied upon by learned counsel for the defendants, being distinguishable on facts and context, is not attracted to the peculiar circumstances of the present case. Quantum and cost of funds

The claim stands reconciled by the two certified statements. The Statement of Account of Istisna Financing (page 469) carries the financing at the full deferred Istisna price, that is, the amount advanced together with the profit fixed for the tenor. It shows a debit balance of Rs.132,335,304.66 as on 18.09.2024, after repayments of Rs.867,272.00, Rs.1,806,318.14 and Rs.3,378,981.00 were adjusted against the earlier balance of Rs.138,387,875.80. The profit embedded in that price is held in the separate account of Deferred Istisna, which shows a credit balance of Rs.40,335,304.66 (page 573). Both statements are extracts of books maintained in the ordinary course of business and, being duly certified, carry the presumption of correctness discussed in para 13. That presumption stands unrebutted. The defendants have not pointed out any entry in either statement or offered any alternative computation, although Sections 10(4) and 10(5) required them to do so. Their objection that profit cannot accrue before the sale of goods goes to the legality of the profit component and not to the arithmetic of the claim. It has been answered in paras 29 to 31, and its bearing on cost of funds is addressed in para 37.

The plaintiff-bank is entitled to cost of funds. Its commencement and base are determined as follows. (i) Entitlement and date of default. Section 3(1) of the Ordinance, 2001 makes it the duty of a customer to fulfil his obligations to the financial institution. Under Section 3(2), a customer who defaults is liable, for the period from the date of his default till realization, to pay the cost of funds of the financial institution as certified by the State Bank of Pakistan. Section 3(3) requires the decree to provide for it, and Section 17(1) includes it in the decree. The provision is mandatory. It creates a substantive pecuniary obligation and must be applied strictly, without liberal construction. Reference can be made to SME Bank Limited through Branch Manager v. Messrs Punjab Store through Proprietor and another (2022 CLD 251). Entitlement therefore follows from the finding of default, and the Court’s task is to determine the date of default and the sum in default. The relevant date is the date on which the financed amount became due and remained unpaid, not merely the expiry or review date of the facility. The offer letter dated 23.10.2023 fixed 30.09.2024 as the validity, expiry or review date, whereas, on the defendants’ own computation (para 26), the individual Istisna transactions carried a tenor of 180 days. The expiry of the facility did not, by itself, accelerate the maturity of transactions already undertaken under it. The plaintiff-bank claims cost of funds from 30.09.2024, but that date cannot be accepted as the date of default, and the claim is declined to that extent. The notice dated 20.12.2024 records that the account had been classified and transferred to the Remedial Assets Management Division. It confirms that the account was overdue by then, but it also afforded a further seven days to discuss the mode of payment and, therefore, does not fix the date of default. The drawdowns were made between 22.05.2024 and 28.06.2024, and even on a 180-day tenor the last of them matured by 25.12.2024 (para 26). By 31.12.2024, therefore, every transaction had matured and remained unpaid, the defendants having neither claimed nor shown any payment thereafter. That date is adopted as the date of default. It is uniform, and it cannot prejudice the defendants, as the earlier transactions matured sooner. (ii) Base. In its prayer clause the plaintiff-bank seeks cost of funds on the total of Rs.132,335,304.66, comprising principal of Rs.92,000,000/- and deferred Istisna income of Rs.40,335,304.66. Cost of funds is awarded as compensation to the financial institution for the finance blocked or stuck up by the customer’s breach, after determining the date of default (SME Bank Limited supra). In Trycot Synthetic Fibre Company through Proprietor and another v. Habib Bank Limited (2012 CLD 1670), a Division Bench of the Sindh High Court restated that nothing beyond the buy-back price may be claimed under an Islamic mode of financing. It nevertheless held that cost of funds is to be calculated on the defaulted sum, that is, the amount not repaid within the contractual period, from the date of commission of default. The sum so treated was the unpaid balance of the total liability, which was inclusive of mark-up. The Istisna price of Rs.132,335,304.66 matured and remained unpaid, and it is the sum in default. The profit was fixed for the tenor of the transactions, all of which had matured by 31.12.2024. The defendants contend that cost of funds on the profit component amounts to mark-up on mark-up. This is not accepted. The Istisna price remains fixed, and the plaintiff- bank is awarded nothing beyond it as a contractual charge, which is the limit recognised in the afore-referred case. Cost of funds is not a contractual addition to the price. It is statutory compensation under Sections 3(2), 3(3) and 17(1) at the State Bank’s certified rate for the period of default, and it is payable on the sum in default irrespective of the mode of finance. (iii) Direction. Cost of funds shall be calculated on Rs.132,335,304.66 from 31.12.2024 until actual realization, at the rate certified by the State Bank of Pakistan from time to time, subject to adjustment of any payments or recoveries made in the meantime. Result

Accordingly, this Court holds that the plaintiff-bank has successfully proved its entitlement to recover the suit amount together with cost of funds till realization. The defendants are jointly and severally liable to satisfy the decree, the defendant-company being liable also to the extent of the mortgaged, hypothecated and charged properties.

For the foregoing reasons, the applications for leave to defend filed by defendants No.1, 3, 4 and 5 and defendant No.2 are dismissed, and the suit is decreed in favour of the plaintiff-bank and against the defendants jointly and severally for a sum of Rs.132,335,304.66 (Rupees One Hundred Thirty-Two Million Three Hundred Thirty-Five Thousand Three Hundred Four and Sixty-Six Paisas Only), along with costs of the suit and cost of funds as envisaged in Section 3 of the Ordinance, 2001, on the defaulted amount from 31.12.2024 till the date of actual realization of the decretal amount. The decretal amount shall be recoverable, inter alia, through the sale of the mortgaged, pledged and hypothecated properties of the defendants, strictly in accordance with law. No relief is granted against the proforma defendants No.6 & 7. Decree sheet be drawn accordingly.

The decree is now converted into execution proceedings under section 19 of the Ordinance, 2001. The decree holder will submit Fard Taleeqa / list of mortgaged, pledged and hypothecated properties of the judgment debtors within a period of thirty days. Execution petition shall be fixed for hearing on 14.12.2026. (Muhammad Sajid Mehmood Sethi) Judge APPROVED FOR REPORTING Judge *Sultan*
